title: Signaling and Cell Cycle
terms: Ordered sequence Gap 1 (G1) → Synthesis (S) → Gap 2 (G2) → Mitosis (M) that makes two daughter cells; cells can exit to G0.
Quiescence: non-dividing cells that have left the cycle.
Growing stage; cell has 1 set of chromosomes.
Growing stage; cell has 2 sets of chromosomes (after replication).
G1 + S + G2 (everything that is not M).
Nuclear envelope disassembles; centrosomes on opposite sides of the cell.
Chromosomes line up on the metaphase plate.
Midline of the cell where chromosomes align during metaphase.
Chromatids on opposite sides; nuclear envelope reforms.
Contractile ring splits the cell; microtubules (MT) form the interphase array.
Ring that pinches the cell in two during cytokinesis.
Structure that duplicates and moves to opposite sides of the cell to organize mitosis.
Point where the cell cycle is regulated; there are three: G1/S, G2/M, M.
Checks growth signals, cell size, DNA damage; proteins involved: pRb, p53, E2F, AKT.
Checks DNA replication, DNA damage, cell size.
Checks spindle attachment and chromosome distribution.
Kinase that integrates multiple signals to decide whether the cell proceeds through a checkpoint.
Three signals: Signal 1 = phosphatase removes a phosphate, Signal 2 = kinase adds a phosphate, Signal 3 = cyclin binds. Inactive → active → move through checkpoint.
Enzyme that removes a phosphate; required step to activate CDK.
'Time-keeper' protein that activates CDK and ensures each step happens in the correct sequence.
Required inputs (usually more than one) for passing the G1/S checkpoint and starting the cycle.
Protein growth signals: EGF, IGF-1, PDGF, EPO.
Growth factor named 'epithelial' on the slide; binds EGFR to drive Ras/MAPK and PI3-K/Akt.
Growth factor listed as a CDK input.
Growth factor listed as a CDK input.
Growth factor listed as a CDK input.
Steroid hormone; signal for female reproductive cell growth.
Steroid hormone; signal for male reproductive cell growth.
Receptor for EGF; becomes phosphorylated (P P) and starts Ras/MAPK and PI3-K/Akt.
Exchange factor that switches Ras from GDP-bound to GTP-bound (active).
Small G protein; inactive with GDP, active with GTP; leads to MAPK.
Kinase downstream of Ras; enters nucleus → Jun/Fos/Myc → transcription of G1 cyclin, G1-CDK, E2F → G1/S progression.
Transcription factors activated by MAPK; drive transcription of G1 cyclin, G1-CDK, and E2F.
Complex activated by growth/environment signals; phosphorylates pRb.
Recruited to phosphorylated EGFR; converts PIP2 → PIP3, which activates PDPK1 and Akt.
Phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate converted to trisphosphate by PI3-K; PIP3 recruits PDPK1 and Akt.
Kinase downstream of PI3-K/PDPK1; INHIBITS apoptosis and cell cycle arrest (T-bars on S12); a G1/S checkpoint protein.
Growth signal that binds Frizzled + LRP and leads to cyclin D transcription.
Phosphorylated after Wnt binding; blocks Axin/GSK3/APC phosphorylation of beta-catenin.
Complex that phosphorylates beta-catenin and sends it to the proteasome when Wnt is absent.
Spared from degradation with Wnt; pairs with LEF/TCF to transcribe cell cycling proteins including cyclin D.
Transcription factors that beta-catenin partners with to transcribe cyclin D.
Broad curve: rises in G1 and stays up across the cycle; output of Wnt/beta-catenin signaling.
Sharp peak at the G1/S boundary.
Rises during S, peaks around the S/G2 boundary.
Peaks at the G2/M boundary, drops in M; with CDK forms mitosis promoting factor.
CDK–cyclin B complex; activity spikes at M each cycle, then falls as cyclin B is degraded.
Active cyclin-CDK triggers the next step AND degradation of the current cyclin, preventing reversal.
Critical control component: binds and inactivates E2F; phosphorylation by G1-CDK–cyclin releases E2F.
Transcription factor for DNA replication genes; released from pRb, travels to nucleus.
Critical control component: phosphorylated by ATM after DNA damage; transcribes p21, which inhibits CDK.
Kinase activated by DNA damage (S15 figure); phosphorylates p53 at the G1/S checkpoint.
CDK inhibitor transcribed by phosphorylated p53; blocks G1-CDK–cyclin.
Early childhood eye tumor where pRb was discovered (source of its name).
Cannot bind E2F → E2F constitutively active → runaway cell division independent of growth signals.
Always on, regardless of upstream signals (here: E2F).
Bone tumor; some carry pRb mutations.
7 yr old greyhound, left front lameness, distal radius swelling, malignant mesenchymal cells with osteoid matrix.
New bone reaction from the periosteum seen on the case radiograph, with palisading cortical bone.
Unmineralized bone matrix made by the malignant cells in the case histology.
traps: pRb binds E2F; p53 does not. p53 acts through p21, which inhibits CDK. Don't swap which molecule binds which (S15).
Phosphorylating pRb RELEASES E2F (turns the brake off). Unphosphorylated pRb = brake on (S15).
CDK activation needs ALL three: bind cyclin + ADD a phosphate + REMOVE a phosphate (phosphatase). Not add OR remove (S9).
Objective: pRb mutations turn the G1/S checkpoint 'permanently on' = the go signal (E2F) is always on / checkpoint bypassed, NOT permanent arrest (S16 vs S18).
G1 = 1 set of chromosomes, G2 = 2 sets. G0 = quiescence (outside the cycle), not a growth phase (S5).
Interphase = G1 + S + G2; it is NOT part of M phase even though S4 lists it with the mitosis terms (S4, S6).
Nuclear envelope disassembles in prometaphase, reforms in telophase. Prophase = condense (S6).
Cyclin B + CDK = mitosis promoting factor. Cyclin D = G1 and the Wnt/beta-catenin output. Don't flip D and B (S13, S14).
G1/S checks growth signals; G2/M checks DNA replication; M checks spindle attachment + chromosome distribution. DNA damage and cell size are checked at BOTH G1/S and G2/M (S8).
Wnt inhibits the Axin/GSK3/APC complex → beta-catenin is spared. Without Wnt, beta-catenin goes to the proteasome (S13). PI3-K makes PIP2 → PIP3, not the reverse (S12).

quiz.stem: A cell has just finished DNA replication and now holds two sets of chromosomes, but mitosis has not begun. Which phase is it in?
quiz.why: G2 is the growing stage with 2 sets of chromosomes; G1 has 1 set, S is replication itself, G0 is quiescence.

quiz.stem: Which phases together make up interphase?
quiz.why: The slide defines interphase as G1, S, + G2; M is mitosis and G0 is outside the cycle.

quiz.stem: During which mitotic stage does the nuclear envelope disassemble while the centrosomes sit on opposite sides of the cell?
quiz.why: Prometaphase = nuclear envelope disassembles, centrosomes on opposite sides (S6 image). Telophase is when the envelope reforms.

quiz.stem: A contractile ring splits the cell and microtubules form the interphase array. Which stage is this?
quiz.why: The slide pairs the contractile ring and the interphase microtubule array with cytokinesis.

quiz.stem: What does the M checkpoint check for?
bad: Growth signals, cell size, and DNA damage
DNA replication, DNA damage, and cell size
Chromosome distribution and completed DNA replication
quiz.why: M checkpoint = spindle attachment + chromosome distribution. DNA replication is G2/M; growth signals are G1/S.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT checked at the G1/S checkpoint?
quiz.why: G1/S checks growth signals, cell size, and DNA damage. Spindle attachment is the M checkpoint.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT required to activate a cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK)?
quiz.why: CDK needs cyclin binding, an added phosphate, and a removed phosphate (phosphatase). Cyclin degradation happens after the step, not to activate it.

quiz.stem: Epithelial growth factor (EGF) binds its receptor, which is phosphorylated and recruits SOS. What happens next?
quiz.why: SOS switches Ras-GDP to Ras-GTP, which leads to mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) → Jun/Fos/Myc → transcription of G1 cyclin, G1-CDK, and E2F.

quiz.stem: Wnt binds Frizzled and LRP, and Disheveled (DVL) is phosphorylated. Which event leads to cyclin D transcription?
bad: APC sends beta-catenin to the proteasome
quiz.why: Disheveled shuts down Axin/GSK3/APC, so beta-catenin survives, partners with LEF/TCF, and transcribes cyclin D.

quiz.stem: Which cyclin forms mitosis promoting factor (MPF) with a cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK)?
quiz.why: The slide labels MPF as the CDK–cyclin B complex.

quiz.stem: What prevents the cell cycle from reversing once a step has been triggered?
quiz.ok: Cyclin-CDK triggers degradation of the current cyclin
bad: p53 triggers degradation of the previous step's cyclin
E2F represses transcription of earlier cyclin genes
pRb binds and sequesters the earlier cyclins
quiz.why: Activated cyclin–cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) complexes trigger the next step and degradation of the current cyclin, so cyclins act as a one-way clock.

quiz.stem: Growth signals activate G1-CDK–cyclin, which phosphorylates the retinoblastoma protein (pRb). What happens next?
quiz.ok: pRb releases E2F, which enters the nucleus
bad: pRb binds E2F more tightly in the cytoplasm
p53 is released and activates p21
p21 is released and inhibits CDK
quiz.why: Phosphorylated pRb lets go of E2F; E2F travels to the nucleus and transcribes DNA replication genes.

quiz.stem: A cell at the G1/S checkpoint has DNA damage. Which sequence stops the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK)?
bad: ATM → p53 → pRb → E2F → CDK inhibited
quiz.why: S15 figure: DNA damage → ATM phosphorylates p53 → p53 transcribes p21 → p21 inhibits G1-CDK–cyclin.

quiz.stem: Which protein binds and inactivates E2F at the G1/S checkpoint?
quiz.why: pRb binds and inactivates E2F, a transcription factor for DNA replication genes.

quiz.stem: A 7-year-old greyhound has a distal radius tumor of malignant mesenchymal cells with osteoid matrix. Its pRb is mutated and cannot bind E2F. What is the effect?
quiz.ok: E2F stays active without growth signals
bad: E2F stays bound and blocks replication
p53 stays active and arrests the cycle
CDK fails to phosphorylate pRb, causing arrest
quiz.why: Mutated Rb cannot bind E2F, so E2F is constitutively active and drives runaway division independent of growth signals.

quiz.stem: An objective states that pRb mutations 'turn the G1/S checkpoint permanently on.' What does this mean mechanistically?
quiz.ok: The E2F go signal is always on
bad: The checkpoint permanently arrests the cell
Growth signals are permanently blocked at G1/S
p53 is permanently activated at G1/S
quiz.why: 'On' means the go signal: E2F is constitutively active, the brake is gone, and the checkpoint is bypassed.

quiz.stem: Which pair are both listed as steroid hormone growth signals?
bad: Testosterone and platelet derived growth factor
quiz.why: Steroid hormones on the slide: estrogen (female reproductive cell growth) and testosterone (male). Erythropoietin and platelet derived growth factor are growth factors.

quiz.stem: Epithelial growth factor (EGF) activates PI3-K, then PDPK1, then Akt (protein kinase B). What does Akt do to the cell?
quiz.ok: Blocks apoptosis and cell cycle arrest
bad: Promotes apoptosis and cell cycle arrest
quiz.why: S12 shows inhibitory T-bars from Akt to apoptosis and to cell cycle arrest: Akt is a pro-growth survival signal.
